name: Technical Demonstrator Architecture
consequences: Prioritizing FIDO2/WebAuthn-based demonstrators accelerates proof-of-concept validation but risks underrepresenting hardware-token scenarios that could challenge OS vendor dominance. A browser-centric approach may limit engagement with mobile-first public services, while GrapheneOS-specific work could isolate the project from broader adoption pathways.
options: Develop a FIDO2/WebAuthn demonstrator targeting GrapheneOS to highlight privacy-respecting alternatives to platform-integrated authentication
Build a browser-based fallback authentication prototype using WebAuthn without OS-level trust anchors to stress-test platform-neutral access
Create a hardware-token integration proof-of-concept demonstrating secure authentication independent of mobile OS integrity signals
review: None of the options fully addresses the risk that technical demonstrators may not align with existing public-sector authentication workflows, creating a gap between innovation and institutional adoption.

name: Policy Framing Strategy
consequences: Focusing on resilience metrics strengthens the case for fallback mechanisms but may dilute the project's sovereignty objectives. Emphasizing supplier concentration risks could provoke resistance from platform vendors, while continuity-of-service arguments might be overshadowed by convenience-focused policymaker priorities.
options: Frame platform neutrality as a resilience requirement tied to national critical infrastructure protection standards
Propose supplier concentration thresholds for public-sector identity systems in procurement contracts
Develop continuity-of-service scenarios demonstrating cascading failures from OS vendor policy changes
review: The options collectively fail to resolve the risk that resilience-focused arguments may not override entrenched convenience priorities in public-sector decision-making.

name: Coalition Engagement Model
consequences: Prioritizing civil-society partnerships strengthens democratic accountability arguments but may limit access to technical decision-makers. Academic collaborations provide credibility but could delay practical implementation, while public-private partnerships risk alignment with incumbent interests.
options: Form a cross-sector coalition including privacy advocates, security researchers, and contingency-planning experts to co-develop technical requirements
Establish a working group with regional municipalities to test fallback authentication scenarios in local public services
Create an academic-industry partnership to publish peer-reviewed analyses of platform dependency risks
review: The options do not adequately address the risk of coalition fragmentation due to conflicting priorities among civil-society, academic, and industry stakeholders.

name: Procurement Influence Mechanism
consequences: Advocating for mandatory platform-neutral clauses in AltID procurement could force systemic change but faces resistance from existing vendors. Pilot programs create low-risk experimentation opportunities but may lack scalability, while third-party audit requirements could delay implementation without ensuring technical outcomes.
options: Insert platform-neutrality requirements into AltID procurement specifications as mandatory compliance criteria
Design pilot programs for fallback authentication in non-critical public services to build operational evidence
Propose independent technical audits of identity system resilience as a precondition for public-sector contracts
review: The options collectively fail to resolve the risk that procurement influence efforts may be circumvented by incrementalism or regulatory capture.

name: EU Standards Alignment Approach
consequences: Engaging with European Digital Identity Wallet frameworks could amplify impact but requires navigating complex EU politics. Focusing on interoperability standards may dilute sovereignty arguments, while emphasizing portability could conflict with national security requirements.
options: Lobby for platform-neutral authentication requirements in European Digital Identity Wallet technical specifications
Develop joint proposals with Nordic counterparts to create regional interoperability benchmarks
Publish comparative analyses of EU and Danish identity frameworks highlighting alignment opportunities
review: The options do not adequately address the risk that EU-level advocacy may be constrained by broader political priorities unrelated to platform neutrality.

name: Contingency Planning Integration
consequences: Embedding fallback scenarios into national contingency plans strengthens institutional commitment but requires navigating bureaucratic inertia. Scenario-based simulations create preparedness but may lack enforcement mechanisms, while regular audit requirements could face resource constraints.
options: Integrate fallback authentication requirements into Denmark's national critical infrastructure contingency plans
Conduct annual simulated disruptions of platform-based authentication to test system resilience
Establish mandatory fallback protocol reviews as part of public-sector IT risk management frameworks
review: The options collectively fail to resolve the risk that contingency planning efforts may remain symbolic without enforceable implementation mechanisms.

name: Stakeholder Communication Protocol
consequences: Prioritizing transparency reports builds public trust but may not influence decision-makers. Technical workshops create knowledge-sharing opportunities but risk exclusion of non-expert stakeholders. Media engagement amplifies visibility but could oversimplify complex technical issues.
options: Publish quarterly transparency reports detailing platform dependency risks and mitigation progress
Host technical workshops with public-sector IT managers to co-design fallback implementation roadmaps
Launch a targeted media campaign emphasizing the national security implications of platform concentration
review: The options do not adequately address the risk that communication efforts may fail to translate technical arguments into actionable policy changes.

name: Resilient Authentication Framework
consequences: Implementing a resilient authentication framework shifts reliance from platform-specific signals to open standards, but requires revalidating trust assumptions across multiple environments. This could delay integration with existing systems if legacy infrastructure lacks compatibility.
options: Develop a FIDO2-based authentication layer decoupled from platform-specific integrity checks
Integrate hardware token validation protocols independent of mobile OS ecosystems
Establish a cross-platform identity verification sandbox for iterative testing
review: The framework's reliance on open standards may not address proprietary system incompatibilities that persist in critical public-sector applications.

name: Standards Ecosystem Development
consequences: Advancing standards ecosystem development positions Denmark as a leader in interoperability, but aligns with EU-wide initiatives that may prioritize broader European interests over national specificity. This could dilute localized requirements.
options: Advocate for FIDO2 and OpenID Connect extensions in eIDAS2 technical working groups
Collaborate with Nordic regulatory bodies to harmonize fallback authentication criteria
Publish open-source reference implementations to accelerate standard adoption
review: The focus on EU alignment might overlook unique Danish operational constraints in public-sector identity management.

name: Supplier Diversification Strategy
consequences: Promoting supplier diversification reduces dependency on Apple/Google, but introduces complexity in managing multiple authentication vendors. This could strain procurement processes if oversight mechanisms are underdeveloped.
options: Pilot alternative authentication providers with non-platform-specific trust models
Create a multi-vendor certification pathway for digital identity solutions
Develop a supplier risk assessment matrix for non-traditional authentication providers
review: The strategy's effectiveness hinges on market readiness of alternative suppliers, which remains uncertain given current industry consolidation.

name: European Regulatory Engagement
consequences: Engaging with European regulatory bodies enhances influence over digital identity frameworks, but diverts resources from direct national policy advocacy. This could slow progress on localized reforms.
options: Submit technical input to the European Digital Identity Wallet working groups
Align Danish fallback requirements with upcoming eIDAS3 regulatory proposals
Organize cross-border workshops with EU member states on platform-neutral authentication
review: The project's impact on EU standards may not directly translate to immediate changes in Danish procurement practices.

name: Coalition Mobilization Strategy
consequences: Mobilizing a diverse coalition strengthens advocacy power, but risks fragmentation if stakeholder priorities conflict. This could dilute the project's core objectives.
options: Form a multi-stakeholder advisory board with civil society and technical experts
Launch a public awareness campaign highlighting supplier concentration risks
Create a joint advocacy platform with privacy organizations and academic institutions
review: The strategy's success depends on maintaining cohesion among stakeholders with differing agendas, which is challenging without centralized leadership.

name: Bureaucratic Engagement Strategy
consequences: Navigating bureaucratic processes ensures compliance and institutional buy-in, but slows down project timelines. This could reduce urgency in addressing immediate dependency risks.
options: Establish regular dialogue channels with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and MitID operators
Develop a structured engagement plan for public-sector procurement committees
Create a formal feedback loop with EU regulatory bodies during standardization processes
review: The strategy's focus on procedural compliance may not address the urgent need for technical and policy interventions.

name: Procurement Policy Integration
consequences: Integrating procurement policy with platform-neutral requirements forces institutional adoption, but faces resistance from vendors reliant on existing ecosystems. This could lead to delayed implementation.
options: Draft procurement clauses mandating fallback authentication capabilities
Work with public-sector buyers to revise tender evaluation criteria
Develop a compliance checklist for platform-neutral identity solutions
review: The strategy's effectiveness is contingent on the willingness of procurement offices to prioritize long-term resilience over short-term vendor convenience.

name: Alternative Authentication Ecosystem Development
consequences: Building open-source authentication protocols reduces reliance on proprietary systems but risks fragmentation without centralized governance. Partnering with Nordic tech firms could accelerate regional adoption but may face legal hurdles from existing platform providers. Creating a public-private certification body establishes credibility but requires sustained political will to enforce standards.
options: Developing open-source authentication protocols compatible with non-Google/Apple platforms
Partnering with Nordic tech firms to co-design alternative authentication frameworks
Creating a public-private certification body for platform-neutral identity solutions
review: Regulatory alignment with EU frameworks remains unaddressed, creating potential conflicts with existing eIDAS2 requirements.

name: Cross-Platform Resilience Testing
consequences: Conducting stress tests on non-Google/Apple systems exposes technical vulnerabilities but may lack institutional credibility without third-party validation. Establishing a sandbox environment for interoperability fosters innovation but requires dedicated funding. Collaborating with EU agencies on shared resilience metrics strengthens advocacy but dilutes focus on national priorities.
options: Conducting independent stress tests on non-Google/Apple authentication systems
Establishing a sandbox environment for cross-platform interoperability experiments
Collaborating with EU agencies to develop shared resilience metrics for digital identity
review: Geopolitical dependencies on foreign tech firms remain unmitigated by technical testing alone.

name: Public Sector Procurement Mandates
consequences: Drafting mandatory platform-neutral clauses in contracts creates legal pressure for change but faces resistance from incumbent vendors. Incentivizing public agencies to adopt alternative systems accelerates adoption but requires budget reallocation. Creating a procurement review panel ensures compliance but adds bureaucratic complexity.
options: Drafting mandatory platform-neutral clauses in public-sector procurement contracts
Incentivizing public agencies to adopt alternative authentication systems through funding tied to compliance
Establishing a procurement review panel to audit digital identity supplier diversity
review: Incumbent vendor lobbying could undermine procurement mandates without explicit political backing.

name: International Standards Advocacy
consequences: Lobbying for global authentication standards positions Denmark as a leader but requires significant diplomatic capital. Engaging with ISO for framework development ensures technical rigor but delays implementation. Hosting international workshops on platform neutrality builds coalitions but risks dilution of national priorities.
options: Lobbying EU institutions to include platform-neutral requirements in digital identity regulations
Engaging with ISO to develop international standards for fallback authentication mechanisms
Hosting international workshops to align Nordic and EU approaches to digital sovereignty
review: Divergent national interests within the EU may slow consensus on unified standards.

name: Citizen Awareness Campaigns
consequences: Launching educational programs on digital sovereignty increases public pressure on policymakers but requires sustained funding. Partnering with media for public discourse amplifies reach but risks oversimplification of technical issues. Developing community workshops fosters grassroots support but may lack institutional influence.
options: Launching targeted educational campaigns on digital sovereignty for public-sector employees
Partnering with national media to create public discourse on platform dependency risks
Developing community workshops to train local leaders in digital identity advocacy
review: Measuring impact on institutional decision-making remains challenging without direct policy engagement.

name: Legacy System Interoperability Framework
consequences: Designing middleware to bridge legacy systems with new authentication models ensures backward compatibility but increases technical complexity. Creating a phased migration plan reduces disruption but extends timelines. Establishing a legacy system audit team identifies vulnerabilities but diverts resources from innovation.
options: Designing middleware solutions to integrate new authentication models with legacy systems
Creating a phased migration plan for public-sector identity infrastructure
Establishing a legacy system audit team to identify critical dependency points
review: Technical debt in legacy systems may limit the effectiveness of new authentication models.

name: Third-Party Audit Infrastructure
consequences: Implementing independent audit mechanisms for authentication systems enhances trust but requires ongoing funding. Creating a certification registry for compliant solutions streamlines adoption but faces resistance from proprietary vendors. Developing a public dashboard for audit results increases transparency but risks information overload.
options: Implementing independent audit mechanisms for all digital identity authentication systems
Creating a certification registry for platform-neutral authentication solutions
Developing a public dashboard to display audit results for digital identity infrastructure
review: Sustaining third-party audit capacity without institutional commitment remains uncertain.
